pages.text: The Amazon rainforest covers more than five million square kilometres across nine countries in South America, with the great majority in Brazil. It is the largest tropical rainforest on earth, containing more species of plant and animal than any other ecosystem on the planet. It produces so much oxygen and absorbs so much carbon dioxide that it has been called the lungs of the earth.

image.note: Map of South America with Amazon basin shaded green, showing scale and nine-country extent

pages.text: The Amazon Basin is named for the River Amazon, the largest river in the world by volume of water. The Amazon carries more water to the sea than the next seven largest rivers combined. It drains a basin the size of Australia. Hundreds of tributaries feed it from the Andes to the west and the central plateau to the south. In the wet season, the Amazon and its tributaries flood enormous areas of forest, creating a seasonal lake that fish swim through among the tree trunks.

The Amazon is not one place. It contains many different habitats: flooded forest, dry forest, savannah, wetland, river, and riverbank. Each habitat has its own community of species, adapted to its specific conditions. The diversity of life within the Amazon is so great that scientists estimate that millions of species have not yet been discovered, named, or described.

The Amazon river system is a world of superlatives with strange details hiding inside them. The river has no bridges along its main stem: it is simply too wide, too deep, and too changeable. In places the opposite bank is barely visible. Where the dark Rio Negro meets the sandy-coloured Amazon near Manaus, the two rivers flow side by side for kilometres without mixing, a two-tone highway of water visible from the air.

The Amazon contains approximately 40,000 plant species, 1,300 bird species, 3,000 types of fish, 430 species of mammals, and more insect species than anyone has managed to count. New species are still being discovered at a rate of several hundred per year.

The jaguar is the largest cat in the Americas and the apex predator of the Amazon. It is a powerful swimmer, unlike most cats, and hunts fish, caiman, and river turtles as well as land animals. Its spotted coat provides camouflage in the dappled light of the forest floor. The jaguar's bite is strong enough to pierce the shells of river turtles and the skulls of prey animals, killing them instantly.

image.note: Illustration of a jaguar at a riverbank, its reflection visible in the water

pages.text: The Amazon river dolphin, or boto, is one of the most unusual animals in the world. It is pink. It lives entirely in fresh water. It has a long beak and can rotate its head almost 180 degrees to navigate among flooded tree trunks. In Amazonian cultures, the boto is a creature of myth and magic, said to transform itself into a handsome person at night and walk among humans.

The poison dart frog is a thumbnail-sized frog that advertises its toxicity with vivid colour: red, blue, yellow, or orange. Its skin secretes some of the most powerful natural toxins known to science. Indigenous Amazonian hunters have used these toxins on the tips of blowpipe darts for generations. Poison dart frogs are not dangerous to handle if the skin is undamaged, but even a tiny amount of their toxin entering the bloodstream can be fatal.

The harpy eagle is the largest eagle in the world. Its wingspan can exceed two metres. It hunts monkeys and sloths in the upper canopy, diving through the trees at speeds that seem impossible given its size. Its talons are the size of a grizzly bear's claws. It mates for life and raises only one chick every two to three years.

The piranha's reputation is mostly slander. These small fish are real, and their teeth are genuinely razor sharp, but most species eat seeds, insects, and other fish, and attacks on healthy swimmers are vanishingly rare. Local children swim in piranha waters daily. The legend of the boiling, flesh-stripping shoal owes more to adventure films than to biology. In the Amazon, as everywhere, the most feared animal is rarely the most dangerous one.

The sloth takes the opposite strategy to almost every animal on earth: it wins by doing less. Moving in slow motion through the canopy, digesting leaves for days at a time, a sloth burns so little energy that it needs only a fraction of the food of a monkey its size. Algae grow in its fur, turning it faintly green and completing its camouflage. Speed attracts eagles. Slowness, done properly, is invisible.

The Amazon has been home to human communities for at least 11,000 years. Today, approximately 400 distinct indigenous groups live in the Amazon, speaking about 300 different languages. They have accumulated extraordinary knowledge of the forest over thousands of years: its plants, animals, medicines, seasonal patterns, and ecosystems.

image.note: Illustration of an indigenous community in the Amazon, showing traditional structures beside a river

pages.text: Some Amazonian communities have chosen to engage with the modern world, living in villages connected by river and road to Brazilian cities, sending children to schools, and participating in the national economy. Others have chosen to remain largely isolated, refusing contact with the outside world. Brazilian law recognises the right of these isolated groups to remain uncontacted, and it is illegal to approach their territories.

Indigenous Amazonian knowledge of medicinal plants has provided some of the most important medicines in modern pharmacology. The muscle relaxant curare, derived from indigenous plant knowledge, became one of the first muscle relaxants used in modern surgery and opened the field of neuromuscular pharmacology. Quinine, the first effective treatment for malaria, came from the bark of the cinchona tree, identified by indigenous peoples of the Andes. Researchers estimate that most of the Amazon's medicinal plants have not yet been investigated by science.

The survival of indigenous people in the Amazon is closely connected to the survival of the forest itself. When the forest is destroyed, indigenous communities lose the land, the resources, and the cultural foundation that makes their way of life possible. Protecting indigenous land rights is therefore one of the most effective ways of protecting the Amazon.

For a period around 1900, the Amazon produced one thing the whole world suddenly wanted: rubber. Fortunes erupted overnight. The jungle city of Manaus built an opera house with materials shipped from Europe, and rubber barons lived in absurd luxury. The boom was built on the brutal exploitation of indigenous and migrant tappers, and it collapsed just as suddenly when rubber plantations were established in Asia. The opera house still stands, a monument to how quickly wealth can come and go.

Modern science reaches the canopy by crane. At research stations in the Amazon, towers and walkways lift scientists forty metres into the treetops, where most of the forest's life actually happens. Up there they have discovered ant species farming fungus gardens, frogs that never touch the ground, and flowers pollinated by a single species of bee. Every expedition returns with something unknown. The canopy has been called the last biological frontier on earth, and it is barely explored.

The Amazon is losing forest at an alarming rate. Deforestation for cattle ranching, soya farming, logging, and mining has destroyed enormous areas in recent decades. At the current rate of destruction, scientists warn that the Amazon is approaching a tipping point: a level of deforestation at which the forest loses its ability to generate its own rainfall, triggering a catastrophic collapse into dry savannah.

This would have consequences far beyond South America. The Amazon influences rainfall patterns across the entire southern half of the continent. It stores an estimated 150 to 200 billion tonnes of carbon. Releasing that carbon through deforestation and burning would accelerate climate change everywhere in the world, including in Nigeria.

image.note: Diagram showing how Amazon moisture release influences rainfall across South America

pages.text: The connection between the Amazon and Nigeria may not be obvious, but it is real. The weather systems that carry moisture from the Atlantic Ocean to Nigeria pass over the Amazon. Changes in the Amazon affect those systems. Nigeria's farmers, who depend on predictable rainfall, are affected by what happens in a forest thousands of kilometres away.

Understanding the Amazon is not only about understanding Brazil or South America. It is about understanding how the earth's systems are connected. The health of one forest affects the health of another. The decisions made in Brasilia affect the weather in Abuja. The world is smaller and more fragile than it looks from any one place.

The Amazon has a sibling. The Congo Basin in Central Africa is the world's second largest rainforest, and its peatlands store more carbon per hectare than almost any landscape on the planet. Africa's great forest faces the same pressures as South America's: logging, mining, and clearing. Nigeria's own rainforest belongs to the same story. Understanding the Amazon is practice for understanding, and defending, the forests closer to home.
